title: What are the JPA inheritance strategies SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED, and TABLE_PER_CLASS? How does each map tables, and what are the trade-offs?

s1_definition.profdef: When you use `@Inheritance` for an entity hierarchy, JPA offers three strategies. `SINGLE_TABLE` (the default) stores the whole hierarchy in **one table** with a discriminator column identifying each row's type; subtype-specific columns are nullable. `JOINED` gives the base class its own table and **each subclass its own table** holding only its extra columns, linked by a shared primary key, so loading a subtype requires a JOIN. `TABLE_PER_CLASS` gives **each concrete subclass its own complete table** (including inherited columns) with no shared base table, so a polymorphic query must UNION across all subclass tables. Each trades off query speed, normalization, and constraint enforcement differently.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine storing savings and current account records. SINGLE_TABLE is one giant ledger book where every account is a row, with a "type" stamp and some columns left blank when they do not apply to that type — fast to read, but messy with blanks. JOINED is a main ledger with the common details, plus a separate thin booklet for savings-only details and another for current-only details, cross-referenced by account number — tidy and no blanks, but you flip between books (join) to see everything. TABLE_PER_CLASS is two entirely separate complete ledgers, one for savings and one for current, each self-contained — simple per type, but "list all accounts" means reading both books and stitching them together (union).
s1_definition.oneliner: SINGLE_TABLE = one table + discriminator (fast, nullable columns); JOINED = base + per-subclass tables joined by key (normalized, join cost); TABLE_PER_CLASS = one full table per concrete class (no base table, union for polymorphic queries).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When you use `@Inheritance` for an entity hierarchy, JPA offers three strategies. `SINGLE_TABLE` (the default) stores the whole hierarchy in **one table** with a discriminator column identifying each row's type; subtype-specific columns are nullable. `JOINED` gives the base class its own table and **each subclass its own table** holding only its extra columns, linked by a shared primary key, so loading a subtype requires a JOIN. `TABLE_PER_CLASS` gives **each concrete subclass its own complete table** (including inherited columns) with no shared base table, so a polymorphic query must UNION across all subclass tables. Each trades off query speed, normalization, and constraint enforcement differently.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine storing savings and current account records. SINGLE_TABLE is one giant ledger book where every account is a row, with a "type" stamp and some columns left blank when they do not apply to that type — fast to read, but messy with blanks. JOINED is a main ledger with the common details, plus a separate thin booklet for savings-only details and another for current-only details, cross-referenced by account number — tidy and no blanks, but you flip between books (join) to see everything. TABLE_PER_CLASS is two entirely separate complete ledgers, one for savings and one for current, each self-contained — simple per type, but "list all accounts" means reading both books and stitching them together (union).

**One line to remember:** SINGLE_TABLE = one table + discriminator (fast, nullable columns); JOINED = base + per-subclass tables joined by key (normalized, join cost); TABLE_PER_CLASS = one full table per concrete class (no base table, union for polymorphic queries).

sections.s2_technical:
`SINGLE_TABLE` is the default and usually the fastest. All subtypes share one table, and a discriminator column (e.g., `account_type`) tells Hibernate which subclass each row is. Queries and polymorphic loads need no joins, so it is the best performer and simplest. The downside: columns that belong only to a subtype must be nullable (a savings-only interest_rate is null for current rows), so you cannot enforce NOT NULL on them at the database level, and a very wide hierarchy produces a sparse table.

```java
@Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.SINGLE_TABLE)
@DiscriminatorColumn(name = "account_type")
```

`JOINED` normalizes the model. The base entity has a table with the common columns; each subclass has a table with only its own extra columns plus a primary key that is also a foreign key to the base table. Inserting a savings account writes one row to the base table and one to the savings table; loading it joins them. This enforces NOT NULL on subtype columns (they live in their own table) and avoids nulls, but every read of a subtype pays a join, and polymorphic queries join across all subclass tables, which can be expensive.

```java
@Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.JOINED)
```

`TABLE_PER_CLASS` gives each *concrete* class a standalone table containing all columns, inherited and own, with no shared base table. Loading a specific subtype is a single-table read with no join. But a polymorphic query against the base type must `UNION ALL` across every subclass table, which is slow and complicates id generation (IDENTITY is problematic because ids must be unique across the union; a shared sequence or table generator is needed). It is the least used strategy.

```java
@Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.TABLE_PER_CLASS)
```

Choosing: default to SINGLE_TABLE for performance and simplicity when subtype-specific NOT NULL constraints are not critical and the hierarchy is not too wide. Choose JOINED when data integrity and normalization matter — many subtype-specific required columns, or a large/variable set of subtypes — and you can tolerate join cost. Avoid TABLE_PER_CLASS unless subtypes are queried in isolation almost always and polymorphic queries are rare.

Senior nuances: SINGLE_TABLE discriminator can be a column or (Hibernate) a formula. JOINED supports `@PrimaryKeyJoinColumn` to name the shared key. TABLE_PER_CLASS cannot use IDENTITY ids. Deep hierarchies in JOINED multiply joins. Second-level cache behaves differently per strategy. And switching strategy later is a schema migration, so decide early based on query patterns and integrity needs.
sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — a wide product hierarchy with many required subtype fields produced a table full of nulls.** At National Bank of India, loan products had many subtype-specific mandatory fields, and putting them all in one SINGLE_TABLE made half the columns null and unenforceable. JOINED gave each subtype its own table with proper NOT NULL constraints. This is exactly the JOINED integrity use case.

**Problem 2 — a high-traffic account lookup needed the fastest possible read with no joins.** The account hierarchy is read constantly and polymorphically, so a join per read would hurt. SINGLE_TABLE reads the whole hierarchy with no join. This is exactly the SINGLE_TABLE performance use case.

What the code will do: show the same Account hierarchy mapped three ways — SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED, and TABLE_PER_CLASS — with the SQL each produces, and a service running a polymorphic query to contrast the generated SQL.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a polymorphic `select a from Account a`, with one savings and one current account.

Step 1 (SINGLE_TABLE) — Hibernate reads the single accounts table once. The account_type discriminator decides which subclass to instantiate per row. There is no join, so this is the fastest. Interest_rate is null on the current row and overdraft_limit is null on the savings row.

Step 2 (JOINED) — Hibernate reads account_base and LEFT JOINs savings_account and current_account on the shared id. Each row assembles its common columns from the base table and its subtype columns from the matching subclass table. No nulls in the subtype tables, but the query carries join cost.

Step 3 (TABLE_PER_CLASS) — Hibernate issues a UNION ALL over savings_full and current_full, each already complete, then treats the union as the Account set. Single-subtype reads are join-free, but this polymorphic query pays the union cost and cannot use IDENTITY ids.

Step 4 — in all three the service receives the same `List<Account>` with the correct subtypes; only the generated SQL and performance differ.

Step 5 — the choice is a schema decision: SINGLE_TABLE for speed and simplicity, JOINED for integrity and normalization, TABLE_PER_CLASS rarely, when subtypes are queried in isolation.

```
2026-10-24 01:25:30 DEBUG Hibernate (SINGLE_TABLE): select a.id, a.account_type, a.balance, a.interest_rate, a.overdraft_limit from accounts a
2026-10-24 01:25:30 INFO  Polymorphic query returned 2 accounts (SQL shape depends on strategy)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  select a from Account a
    │
    ├─ SINGLE_TABLE ──→ accounts (1 table + account_type)   NO JOIN fastest
    │                     interest_rate/overdraft_limit nullable
    │
    ├─ JOINED ────────→ account_base ⋈ savings_account      JOIN per subtype
    │                               ⋈ current_account        NOT NULL enforceable
    │
    └─ TABLE_PER_CLASS → savings_full UNION ALL current_full UNION (slow poly)
                           each table complete, no base       IDENTITY not allowed
    ▼
  List<Account> with correct subtypes (same result, different SQL/perf)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — SINGLE_TABLE vs JOINED vs TABLE_PER_CLASS (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy (persistence layout chosen per hierarchy)         │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  O: swap strategy annotation without changing domain code   │
  │  L: all subtypes substitutable wherever Account is used     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Table Layout (as prose) ──
  SINGLE_TABLE: accounts(id, account_type[disc], balance, interest_rate?, overdraft_limit?)
     + fastest reads, no joins  − nullable subtype cols, sparse wide table
  JOINED: account_base(id,balance) + savings_account(id→base, interest_rate NOT NULL)
          + current_account(id→base, overdraft_limit NOT NULL)
     + normalized, enforce NOT NULL  − join per read, costly polymorphic queries
  TABLE_PER_CLASS: savings_full(all cols) + current_full(all cols), NO base table
     + single-subtype reads join-free  − UNION for polymorphic, no IDENTITY ids

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. same JPQL select from Account
  2. Hibernate emits SQL per strategy (scan / join / union)
  3. discriminator or table source → subtype instances

  (Caution) TABLE_PER_CLASS can't use IDENTITY. (Caution) deep JOINED hierarchies multiply joins.
  Rule: default SINGLE_TABLE; JOINED for integrity; TABLE_PER_CLASS rarely.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When I use inheritance for an entity hierarchy, JPA gives me three strategies and they are really a choice about the database layout. Single table, the default, stores the whole hierarchy in one table with a discriminator column that identifies each row's type, and subtype-specific columns are nullable. It is the fastest because queries and polymorphic loads need no joins, and it is the simplest, but the cost is that subtype-only columns must be nullable so I cannot enforce not-null on them at the database level, and a wide hierarchy produces a sparse table full of blanks.

Joined normalizes the model: the base class gets a table with the common columns, and each subclass gets its own table holding only its extra columns, linked by a primary key that is also a foreign key to the base. This lets me enforce not-null on subtype columns because they live in their own tables, and it avoids nulls, but every read of a subtype pays a join, and a polymorphic query joins across all the subclass tables, which can be expensive. Table per class gives each concrete subclass its own complete, standalone table with no shared base, so a single-subtype read is a plain table scan with no join, but a polymorphic query against the base must union across every subclass table, which is slow, and it cannot use identity id generation because ids must be unique across the union.

At National Bank of India I made this choice based on query patterns and integrity needs. Our account hierarchy is read constantly and polymorphically, and a join per read would hurt, so I kept it on single table for the fastest no-join reads, accepting a couple of nullable subtype columns. But our loan products had many subtype-specific mandatory fields, and single table would have produced a table full of unenforceable nulls, so for that hierarchy I used joined so each subtype has its own table with proper not-null constraints. I almost never use table per class, reserving it for the rare case where subtypes are queried in isolation and polymorphic queries are rare. The nuances I always mention are that single table can use a discriminator column or formula, that joined can name the shared key with a primary-key join column, that table per class rules out identity ids so I use a sequence or table generator, and that changing strategy later is a schema migration, so I decide early.

---

keyPoints: SINGLE_TABLE: all types in one table + discriminator column — fastest queries
JOINED: each type in own table, JOINs for queries — normalized, slower
TABLE_PER_CLASS: each concrete class gets full table — no joins, but union queries
SINGLE_TABLE default — best performance, wastes some space with null columns
